title: China Forced Nepal to Cancel an International Conference on Tibetan Studies - The Diplomat – Asia
description: China Forced Nepal to Cancel an International Conference on Tibetan Studies  The Diplomat – Asia
publisher.title: The Diplomat – Asia
full_article:
The 17th Seminar of the International Association for Tibetan Studies (IATS) Conference, scheduled to be held at Kathmandu University, Nepal, from August 23-29, was cancelled on August 5 and later shifted online . The cancellation was done by the organizers, at the formal request of the Nepali government.

The IATS conference is one of the premier academic forums for Tibetan culture, history, language and religion. The conference was set to bring together scholars from 40 countries , including India, China, and the United States – many of whom had already arranged and paid for costs to attend the conference in Kathmandu. The conference had been in planning for four years, as Nepal was selected to host the seminar in 2022. The abrupt cancellation of the conference on grounds of “security concerns” highlights both Beijing’s ironclad grip and bid to assert authority over Tibetan Buddhism.

The cancellation came after Chinese officials expressed concerns over pro-Tibet activists using the platform for demonstrations. Notably, Nepal’s security agencies had ruled out the possibility of a security threat to the event.

The pressure came not only from Chinese diplomats but, most remarkably, a religious figure. The Venerable Master Yinshun, former vice president of the Buddhist Association of China and a member of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) and abbot of the Chinese Temple of Nepal, visited Nepal on July 29. Following his visit, combined with diplomatic efforts by Chinese Ambassador to Nepal Zhang Maoming, around a dozen scholars from the Tibetan Policy Institute in India withdrew their participation from the conference.

The cancellation of the conference is consistent with Beijing’s recent efforts to exert control over Nepal’s association with Tibetan Buddhism. This is seen in several pre-emptive and proactive measures taken by Beijing to curb Tibetan Buddhism’s influence in Nepal. Earlier this year, Zhang, China’s ambassador, warned the home minister of Nepal, Sudan Gurung, against any government-level participation by Nepal in the oath-taking ceremony of the penpa tshering held on May 27 in Dharamshala, India. The penpa tshering is the highest executive authority of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA). Notably, the oath-taking ceremony was also attended by the 14th Dalai Lama.

The CTA functions as the government-in-exile for the Tibetan people globally. Around 91,000 Tibetans registered their vote for the 2026 elections that elected the penpa tshering across India, Nepal, Bhutan, Europe, the United States, and other parts of Asia and Africa. In a bid to delegitimize the elections and the support for the CTA, a Global Times editorial characterized the elections as illegal and the CTA as an illicit “separatist organization.”

These efforts are not unique to Nepal. China has accelerated its efforts seeking to control narratives and perceptions related to Tibet around the world. Beijing’s bid for control over Tibetan Buddhism in particular comes at a crucial time: the Dalai Lama is now 91 years old, and he has announced that his trust, the Gaden Phodrang, would have the sole authority in recognizing his future reincarnation. Beijing responded swiftly, maintaining that the selection of the Dalai Lama’s successor would be determined by Chinese law.

The succession of the 14th Dalai Lama poses a strategic challenge to China. The Himalayan landscape spanning across India and China has been the site of border disputes between India and China, most recently the Galwan clashes of 2020. Many locals of the Himalayan region in the states of Sikkim, Ladakh, and Arunachal Pradesh in India are adherents of the Tibetan strand of Buddhism. Notably the Dalai Lama celebrated his 91st birthday in Ladakh – a demonstration of the expanse of influence of the Tibetan strand of Buddhism over the Indian Himalayan landscape.

The long-established cultural traditions of the locals of the Himalayan region, along with their reverence and faith in the Dalai Lama, delegitimize Chinese claims of normative authority in dictating Tibetan Buddhist practices. China has consistently maintained that the next Dalai Lama will be born in Chinese territory as opposed to the 14th Dalai Lama’s declaration that the next Dalai Lama may be born in India.

In recent times, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has shown increased attention toward the management of monasteries in its bid to establish control over the Tibetan strand of Buddhism. The CCP has taken on a more intrusive role, as seen during Li Ganjie’s tour of Gansu and Sichuan earlier this year. Li heads the United Front Work Department (UFWD). During the tour, he emphasized legal, standardized management of Tibetan Buddhist institutions and the need for socialist principles to guide Tibetan Buddhism.

One of the primary tasks of the UFWD in China is to generate favorable receptions for Chinese policies not only domestically but also overseas. In this context, Li’s interest in the management of monasteries is geared toward enhancing the CCP’s control over perceptions of Tibetan Buddhism both at home and abroad.

In many ways, its attempts to control Tibetan Buddhism expose the CCP’s discomfort with religion in general. An increasing number of the urban middle class in China are turning to religious and spiritual practices. Following the COVID-19 pandemic, a growing number of individuals in China have been attracted to the sense of community that religion provides. Chinese Buddhist institutions are perceived by many as corrupt and criticized for excessive commercialization, whereas Tibetan Buddhism is viewed as more esoteric. This sentiment has grown over the years with the rise in cases of embezzlement and corruption in Chinese Buddhist monasteries and temples. A rising number of the younger population in China are attracted to the day to day practices in Tibetan Buddhism as a key to a more balanced lifestyle.

नेपाल के काठमांडू विश्वविद्यालय में 23-29 अगस्त तक होबय वाला इंटरनेशनल एसोसिएशन फॉर तिब्बती स्टडीज (IATS) सम्मेलन के 17म गोष्ठी 5 अगस्त के रद्द भ गेल छल आ बाद में ऑनलाइन शिफ्ट भ गेल छल . रद्दीकरण आयोजक द्वारा, नेपाली सरकारक औपचारिक आग्रह पर कयल गेल अछि ।

आईएटीएस सम्मेलन तिब्बती संस्कृति, इतिहास, भाषा आरू धर्म केरऽ प्रमुख शैक्षणिक मंचऽ म॑ स॑ एक छै । सम्मेलन में भारत, चीन, आ अमेरिका सहित 40 देश के विद्वान सब के एक संग आबय के छल – जाहि में सं बहुतो गोटे काठमांडू में सम्मेलन में भाग लेबय के व्यवस्था आ खर्च के भुगतान क चुकल छलाह. सम्मेलन केरऽ योजना चारि साल स॑ छेलै, कैन्हेंकि नेपाल क॑ २०२२ म॑ ई गोष्ठी के मेजबानी लेली चुनलऽ गेलऽ छेलै ।“सुरक्षा सरोकार” के आधार प॑ सम्मेलन केरऽ अचानक रद्द होना बीजिंग केरऽ लोहा केरऽ पकड़ आरू तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म प॑ अधिकार केरऽ दावा दूनू क॑ उजागर करै छै ।

चीनी अधिकारी सिनी न॑ तिब्बत समर्थक कार्यकर्ता सिनी न॑ ई मंच के प्रदर्शन लेली इस्तेमाल करै प॑ चिंता व्यक्त करला के बाद ई रद्द करलऽ गेलऽ छै । उल्लेखनीय अछि जे नेपाल के सुरक्षा एजेंसी एहि आयोजन पर सुरक्षा खतरा के संभावना के खारिज क देने छल.

ई दबाव चीनी राजनयिकऽ के ही नै बल्कि सबसें उल्लेखनीय बात ई छेलै कि एगो धार्मिक हस्ती के तरफऽ स॑ भी आबी गेलऽ छेलै । चीन के बौद्ध संघ के पूर्व उपाध्यक्ष आरू चीनी जन राजनीतिक परामर्शदात्री सम्मेलन (सीपीपीसीसी) के राष्ट्रीय समिति के सदस्य आरू नेपाल के चीनी मंदिर के मठाधीश पूज्य मास्टर यिनशुन 29 जुलाई क॑ नेपाल के दौरा करलकै भारत मे संस्थान सम्मेलन स अपन भागीदारी वापस ल लेलक।

सम्मेलन रद्द करब बीजिंग केरऽ हाल केरऽ प्रयास के अनुरूप छै कि नेपाल केरऽ तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म के साथ जुड़ाव प॑ नियंत्रण रखै के कोशिश करलऽ जाय । ई बात नेपाल म॑ तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म केरऽ प्रभाव प॑ लगाम लगाबै लेली बीजिंग द्वारा करलऽ गेलऽ कईएक पूर्वाग्रही आरू सक्रिय उपायऽ म॑ देखलऽ जाय छै । एहि सालक शुरुआत मे चीनक राजदूत झांग नेपालक गृहमंत्री सूडान गुरुंग केँ भारतक धर्मशाला मे 27 मई केँ आयोजित पेनपा त्शेरिंगक शपथ ग्रहण समारोह मे नेपालक कोनो तरहक सरकारी स्तरीय भागीदारी सँ चेतावनी देलनि। पेनपा त्शेरिंग केंद्रीय तिब्बती प्रशासन (सीटीए) केरऽ सर्वोच्च कार्यकारी प्राधिकारी छेकै । उल्लेखनीय अछि जे शपथ ग्रहण समारोह मे 14म दलाई लामा सेहो शामिल छलाह।

सीटीए वैश्विक स्तर पर तिब्बती लोगऽ लेली निर्वासित सरकार के रूप म॑ काम करै छै । २०२६ केरऽ चुनाव लेली लगभग ९१,००० तिब्बती न॑ अपनऽ वोट दर्ज करलकै जेकरा म॑ पूरा भारत, नेपाल, भूटान, यूरोप, अमेरिका, आरू एशिया आरू अफ्रीका केरऽ अन्य भागऽ म॑ पेनपा त्शेरिंग के चुनाव करलऽ गेलै । चुनाव आरू सीटीए केरऽ समर्थन क॑ अवैध बनाबै के कोशिश म॑ ग्लोबल टाइम्स केरऽ एगो संपादकीय म॑ चुनाव क॑ गैरकानूनी आरू सीटीए क॑ गैरकानूनी “अलगाववादी संगठन” के रूप म॑ पेश करलऽ गेलऽ छै ।

ई प्रयास नेपालक लेल विशिष्ट नहि अछि । चीन न॑ दुनिया भर म॑ तिब्बत स॑ जुड़लऽ कथ्य आरू धारणा प॑ नियंत्रण रखै के कोशिश म॑ अपनऽ प्रयास म॑ तेजी लानल॑ छै । खास करी क॑ तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म प॑ नियंत्रण लेली बीजिंग केरऽ दावेदारी एगो महत्वपूर्ण समय म॑ आबी रहलऽ छै : दलाई लामा केरऽ उम्र अब॑ ९१ साल होय गेलऽ छै, आरू हुनी घोषणा करी देल॑ छै कि हुनकऽ भविष्य केरऽ पुनर्जन्म क॑ पहचानै के एकमात्र अधिकार हुनकऽ ट्रस्ट, गडेन फोड्रंग क॑ होतै । बीजिंग न॑ तेजी स॑ जवाब देलकै आरू कहलकै कि दलाई लामा केरऽ उत्तराधिकारी के चयन चीनी कानून स॑ तय करलऽ जैतै ।

14म दलाई लामा के उत्तराधिकार चीन के लेल रणनीतिक चुनौती अछि. भारत आरू चीन भर म॑ फैललऽ हिमालय केरऽ परिदृश्य भारत आरू चीन के बीच सीमा विवाद के स्थल रहलऽ छै, जेकरा म॑ सबसें हाल म॑ २०२० केरऽ गलवान झड़प छेलै ।भारत केरऽ सिक्किम, लद्दाख, आरू अरुणाचल प्रदेश राज्यऽ के हिमालय क्षेत्र केरऽ बहुत सारा स्थानीय लोग बौद्ध धर्म केरऽ तिब्बती स्ट्रैंड के अनुयायी छै । उल्लेखनीय छै कि दलाई लामा न॑ लद्दाख म॑ अपनऽ ९१वां जन्मदिन मनाबै छेलै – जे भारतीय हिमालयी परिदृश्य प॑ बौद्ध धर्म केरऽ तिब्बती स्ट्रैंड केरऽ प्रभाव के विस्तार के प्रदर्शन छेलै ।

हिमालयी क्षेत्र के स्थानीय लोगऽ के लंबा समय स॑ स्थापित सांस्कृतिक परंपरा के साथ-साथ दलाई लामा के प्रति हुनकऽ श्रद्धा आरू विश्वास तिब्बती बौद्ध प्रथा के हुकुम लगाबै म॑ चीनी के मानक अधिकार के दावा क॑ वैधताहीन करी दै छै । चीन लगातार ई बात के कहना छै कि अगला दलाई लामा के जन्म चीनी इलाका म॑ होतै जेकरऽ विपरीत 14वां दलाई लामा केरऽ घोषणा छै कि अगला दलाई लामा के जन्म भारत म॑ होय सकै छै ।

हाल के समय म॑ चीनी कम्युनिस्ट पार्टी (सीसीपी) न॑ बौद्ध धर्म केरऽ तिब्बती स्ट्रैंड प॑ नियंत्रण स्थापित करै के कोशिश म॑ मठऽ के प्रबंधन के तरफ बढ़लऽ ध्यान देखैलकै । सीसीपी न॑ आरू घुसपैठिया भूमिका निभैल॑ छै, जैसनऽ कि ई साल केरऽ शुरुआत म॑ ली गंजी केरऽ गांसू आरू सिचुआन केरऽ दौरा के दौरान देखलऽ गेलऽ छेलै । ली संयुक्त मोर्चा कार्य विभाग (यूएफडब्ल्यूडी) के प्रमुख छैथ। भ्रमण के दौरान हुनी तिब्बती बौद्ध संस्थानऽ के कानूनी, मानकीकृत प्रबंधन आरू तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म के मार्गदर्शन लेली समाजवादी सिद्धांतऽ के जरूरत प॑ जोर देलकै ।

चीन म॑ यूएफडब्ल्यूडी केरऽ एगो प्राथमिक काम चीनी नीति लेली न सिर्फ घरेलू स्तर प॑ बल्कि विदेशऽ म॑ भी अनुकूल स्वागत पैदा करना छै । ई संदर्भ म॑ मठऽ के प्रबंधन म॑ ली केरऽ रुचि देश आरू विदेश दूनू जगह प॑ तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म केरऽ धारणा प॑ सीसीपी केरऽ नियंत्रण बढ़ाबै के दिशा म॑ छै ।

बहुत तरह स॑ तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म प॑ नियंत्रण रखै के ओकरऽ प्रयास स॑ सीसीपी केरऽ सामान्य रूप स॑ धर्म के प्रति असुविधा के खुलासा होय छै । चीन केरऽ शहरी मध्यम वर्ग केरऽ बढ़तऽ संख्या धार्मिक आरू आध्यात्मिक प्रथा के तरफ रुख करी रहलऽ छै । कोविड-19 महामारी के बाद चीन में बढ़ैत संख्या में व्यक्ति के ओहि समुदाय के भाव के प्रति आकर्षित कयल गेल अछि जे धर्म प्रदान करैत अछि | चीनी बौद्ध संस्थान क॑ बहुत लोगऽ द्वारा भ्रष्ट मानलऽ जाय छै आरू अत्यधिक व्यावसायिकरण के कारण आलोचना करलऽ जाय छै, जबकि तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म क॑ अधिक गूढ़ मानलऽ जाय छै । चीनी बौद्ध मठ आरू मंदिरऽ म॑ गबन आरू भ्रष्टाचार के मामला बढ़ला के साथ ई भावना वर्षो स॑ बढ़ी गेलऽ छै । चीन केरऽ बढ़तऽ संख्या म॑ युवा आबादी तिब्बती बौद्ध धर्म म॑ रोजमर्रा के प्रथा के तरफ आकर्षित होय रहलऽ छै जे अधिक संतुलित जीवनशैली के कुंजी छै ।

title: WHO-Lions Clubs partner to expand mental health services in Jordan and Nepal - World Health Organization (WHO)
description: WHO-Lions Clubs partner to expand mental health services in Jordan and Nepal  World Health Organization (WHO)
publisher.title: World Health Organization (WHO)
full_article:
14 August 2026: Globally, more than 1 billion people live with a mental health condition. Yet, in many countries access to mental health care is extremely limited. Responding to this need, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Lions Clubs International Foundation (LCIF) have signed a three-year agreement to increase access to care for people living with mental, neurological and substance use conditions in Jordan and Nepal as part of the WHO Special Initiative for Mental Health. The partnership offers important potential to raise awareness about mental health, encourage help-seeking and to leverage the global and local influence of both organizations.

Recognizing the growing need to promote mental health and well-being, Lions Clubs International (LCI) has identified mental health as one of its global initiatives. “I am proud to see Lions helping reduce stigma, raise awareness, and expand access to care in communities around the world,” said A.P Singh, LCIF Chairperson.

In Jordan’s East Amman areas, the partnership will expand access to mental health care by establishing counselling services in collaboration with the Friends of Cancer Patients Association and delivering acute secondary care for children and adults at the Al Basheer Hospital.

In Nepal, the partnership will establish psychosocial support mental health corners in 10 district hospitals and strengthen young people’s mental health through implementation of the Nepal government-endorsed National Implementation Framework on School Mental Health.

“The treatment gap for people living with mental health conditions can be over 95% in some countries,” said Dr Mark van Ommeren, Head of WHO’s Mental Health and Substance Use Unit . “This Lions Club International and WHO Special Initiative for Mental Health joint effort is a great example of how we can collaborate and work towards common goals.”

This partnership will continue until the end of 2028, documenting service users’ stories and experiences throughout its implementation.

Note for editors

WHO’s Special Initiative for Mental Health

The WHO Special Initiative for Mental Health (SIMH) scales up community-based mental health care and works to advance national policies, plans and laws to protect and support people living with mental, neurological and substance use conditions, and ensure the inclusion of mental health care as part of universal health coverage. Since 2019 the SIMH has expanded mental health care across ten countries where more than 90 million additional people now have access to community-based mental health care; and at least 2 million children and adults have received treatment for mental, neurological and substance use conditions for the first time. Countries, including Jordan and Nepal, have advanced rights-based mental health policies, updated essential medicine lists, improved mental health data systems, integrated mental health into emergency preparedness plans, and continue to advocate for increased domestic investment to sustain progress. For further information on the WHO SIMH, contact: MHSunit@who.int

Lions Clubs International Foundation

The Lions Clubs International Foundation (LCIF) is the global foundation supporting the 1.4 million members of Lions Clubs International through grant funds that expand their compassionate works and empower their service at home and around the world. Since its founding in 1968, LCIF has awarded more than 25 000 grants totaling more than US$ 1.3 billion. We improve health and well-being, strengthen communities and support those in need, locally and globally. Learn more about who we are and what we do at lionsclubs.org/lcif or donate to LCIF at lionsclubs.org/donate. Follow LCIF on Facebook at @LCIFLions.

Jordan, Malak Nowfal, Housewife and Carer. “My name is Malak, I’m 28 years old, and I’m the wife of Fouad. The Special Initiative for Mental Health played a significant role in both of our journeys. It wasn’t just about helping those with mental health conditions it was also about helping the people who support them. It felt like, finally, there was a space in society for us, where we weren’t alone in this journey. I began to feel seen and empowered, and more importantly, so did Fouad. Mental illness is often misunderstood as something to fear. But I’ve come to believe, and I wish more people would, that mental health matters just as much as physical health.” © WHO, 2025

१४ अगस्त २०२६ : वैश्विक स्तर पर १ अरब स॑ भी अधिक लोग मानसिक स्वास्थ्य केरऽ स्थिति के साथ जीबै छै । तइयो, बहुत सं देशक मे मानसिक स्वास्थ्य देखभाल कें पहुंच अत्यंत सीमित छै. ई आवश्यकता के जवाब दैत विश्व स्वास्थ्य संगठन (डब्ल्यूएचओ) आरू लायंस क्लब इंटरनेशनल फाउंडेशन (एलसीआईएफ) न॑ डब्ल्यूएचओ केरऽ मानसिक स्वास्थ्य लेली विशेष पहल के तहत जॉर्डन आरू नेपाल म॑ मानसिक, न्यूरोलॉजिकल आरू मादक पदार्थ के उपयोग के स्थिति स॑ पीड़ित लोगऽ के देखभाल के पहुँच बढ़ाबै लेली तीन साल के समझौता प॑ हस्ताक्षर करलकै । इ साझेदारी मानसिक स्वास्थ्य कें बारे मे जागरूकता पैदा करय, मदद कें मांग कें प्रोत्साहित करय आ दूनू संगठनक कें वैश्विक आ स्थानीय प्रभाव कें लाभ उठावा कें लेल महत्वपूर्ण संभावना प्रदान करयत छै.

मानसिक स्वास्थ्य आरू भलाई क॑ बढ़ावा दै के बढ़तऽ जरूरत क॑ पहचानी क॑ लायंस क्लब इंटरनेशनल (एलसीआई) न॑ मानसिक स्वास्थ्य क॑ अपनऽ वैश्विक पहलऽ म॑ स॑ एक के रूप म॑ पहचान करलकै । एलसीआईएफ कें अध्यक्ष ए.पी.

जॉर्डन केरऽ पूर्वी अम्मान क्षेत्रऽ म॑ ई साझेदारी फ्रेंड्स ऑफ कैंसर मरीज संघ के सहयोग स॑ परामर्श सेवा स्थापित करी क॑ आरू अल बशीर अस्पताल म॑ बच्चा आरू वयस्कऽ लेली तीव्र माध्यमिक देखभाल प्रदान करी क॑ मानसिक स्वास्थ्य देखभाल के पहुँच के विस्तार करतै ।

डब्ल्यूएचओ केरऽ मानसिक स्वास्थ्य आरू पदार्थ केरऽ उपयोग इकाई केरऽ प्रमुख डॉ. मार्क वैन ओमेरेन न॑ कहलकै कि मानसिक स्वास्थ्य केरऽ स्थिति स॑ पीड़ित लोगऽ लेली इलाज के अंतर कुछ देशऽ म॑ ९५% स॑ भी अधिक होय सकै छै । “लायंस क्लब इंटरनेशनल आरू डब्ल्यूएचओ स्पेशल इनिशिएटिव फॉर मेंटल हेल्थ केरऽ ई संयुक्त प्रयास एकरऽ एगो बढ़िया उदाहरण छै कि हम्मं॑ कोना सहयोग करी सकै छियै आरू साझा लक्ष्य के दिशा म॑ काम करी सकै छियै।”

full_article:
A historic military tradition between India and Nepal is facing an uncertain future. Gorkha veterans are reportedly demanding that Kathmandu clears the way for Nepali youths to join the Indian Army again. According to a Nepali news portal in the central Nepalese city of Pokhara, former Gorkha soldiers and their supporters took to the streets calling for recruitment to resume under India's Agnipath scheme.



The protest was reportedly organised by the Indian ex-servicemen Gorkha brigade Nepal Pokhara. It also comes just days before Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth is scheduled to visit Nepal. According to the Nepalese news portal, the group submitted a two-point memorandum to Nepal's federal government through the district administration office. They are demanding the immediate restart of recruitment. The protesters reportedly say the recruitment freeze has cost Nepali youths an important employment opportunity while putting a centuries-old military tradition at risk.



Nepali youths have been recruited into the Indian Army for more than two centuries following a treaty signed between the British East India Company and the Kingdom of Nepal in 1816. After India's Independence in 1947, six Gorkha regiments of the British Indian Army became part of the Indian Army under a tripartite agreement involving India, Nepal and Britain. They are said to be the fiercest fighters on the planet. Ferocious warriors who can guarantee you a win. Famous for their slouch hats and curved kukri knives, they have served many armies, fought multiple battles and won numerous awards both under British rule and the Indian Army.

full_article:
When he is not meeting with Nepal’s new foreign minister Shisir Khanal, to think through policy, 26-year-old Nikhil Sangroula (GU-Q ‘23) sits at his desk inside the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, looking out at the dome of the new parliament building across the street. Below, first-time lawmakers move quickly between meetings, with a sense of momentum that feels new.

“It is highly spirited in the bureaucratic class,” Sangroula said. “There is a fresh, vibrant energy in the administrative halls. Innovation and partnership are open in an unprecedented manner. I get to speak with young bureaucrats, mostly Gen Z, who are equally hopeful that this leadership will lead them to a better tomorrow. There is no chance, no option, for this government to fail. This is a turning moment for us.”

But every time he looks out that window, he remembers September 2025.

A government ban on social media set off protests that spread across the country. Streets filled with fires and broken storefronts. In a single day on September 8, state security forces killed 19 young protesters in broad daylight. Then, within hours, former prime minister K P Sharma Oli resigned, and Nepal was left without clear leadership.

“The state’s failure to manage the situation, and the lives lost, mostly bystanders, was a genuine tragedy,” Sangroula said. “Having lived through it, my hope is simply that Nepal never has to go through anything like it again.”

Out of that moment came the youngest government in the world right now, led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah, at just 36 years old.

Three years after graduating from Georgetown University in Qatar (GUQ), Sangroula now works close to its centre as a Co-ordination, Implementation and Monitoring Officer in the Foreign Minister’s Secretariat.

He supports the foreign minister’s research and analysis, helps draft speeches, and connects communities and experts with the ministry. A key part of his role is gathering data to support proposed policies.

Sangroula grew up far from Kathmandu’s political circles. He was born and raised in Jhapa, in Nepal’s eastern lowlands, where his parents treated education as a necessity. That commitment to learning eventually took him far beyond Nepal’s borders. He went to Doha, where he studied Arabic, majored in international economics and minored in government at GU-Q.

“Nepalis have migrated across the globe in search of opportunity, and they demonstrate a genuine acceptance, a willingness to welcome people of every belief without simply tolerating them,” he said.

That belief in building bridges shaped his path after graduation. Sangroula joined the Nepal Leadership Academy, where he helped design workshops for emerging political leaders and supported a cross-party caucus focused on collaboration. Some of those same figures now are the members of parliament.

Inside the ministry, Sangroula leads its first internship and fellowship program, bringing early-career professionals into public service. He sees a generation less focused on ideology and more focused on results, impatient for better governance, but still learning how the state moves.

“The country has a lot more aspiration for efficient public service delivery and stable politics,” he said. “People are looking for swift delivery on outcomes of development. In general, people are not looking for ideology or abstractions. There is strong demand for good governance and economic development.”

He does not see youth alone as the answer. What changed, he said, was a growing exhaustion with stagnation.

“In my interaction with bureaucrats who have lived through this transition, there is a lot of energy, vitality and proactiveness in the new political class leading the nation today,” he said. “Age is definitely a factor, but even more so were a few octogenarian leaders who had been in power for a long time, and their passivity, which led to discontent for a long time.”

For GU-Q students considering public service, his advice: “A lot of people our age want fast, visible change. But every state is inherently conservative in how it moves. If you want change, you need to build consensus and bring people along. The impact of working with government is slower, but it lasts.”

full_article:
The European Union marked International Youth Day in Nepal on Thursday with a full day of events in Kathmandu linking scholarships, skills training and youth-led projects.

Activities were held at Hotel Malla and brought together students, Erasmus scholars and alumni, entrepreneurs, civil society organisations, innovators, private-sector partners and youth leaders, the EU Delegation to Nepal announced on Friday, cited by the European External Action Service (EEAS).

The programme combined an Erasmus Mundus pre-departure orientation, an EU Youth Fest and an EU Youth Alumni Day.

EU Ambassador to Nepal Véronique Lorenzo congratulated 42 Nepali students who have secured Erasmus Mundus Joint Master Degree scholarships to study at universities across the EU.

The recipients included 22 women and 20 men, and will study subjects such as public health, cybersecurity, journalism, renewable energy and sustainable construction.

More than 1,500 young people attended the EU Youth Fest 2026, where participants received guidance and mentorship from professionals and tried activities including 3D modelling and printing, drone simulations and AI-powered games.

The event also introduced emerging industries including animation, robotics and artificial intelligence.

New grants worth €1.91 million announced

Two new grants worth a combined €1.91 million were launched at the festival — Creating Opportunities for Youth in Digital Economy (CODE) and Unleashing Digital Acceleration and Ambition of Nepali Youth (UDAAN), the Delegation said.

CODE will be implemented by Swisscontact, Restless Development and the Robotics Association of Nepal, while UDAAN will be delivered by Youth Innovation Lab, Women in Animation, Heifer Project Nepal and the Nepal Applied Mathematics and Informatics Institute for Research (NAAMII).

The initiatives will engage young people across Nepal’s seven provinces, focusing on digital skills, employability, entrepreneurship and innovation, with particular attention on young women, rural communities, and vulnerable and marginalised groups.

“One of Nepal's greatest resources is its youth,” Lorenzo said. “But this potential must be matched by investment in skills, opportunity, and employment,” she added.

The EU also held an EU Youth Alumni Day, bringing together alumni, youth organisations and partners to showcase youth-led initiatives in areas including the circular economy, green growth, education, climate action and youth participation.

होटल मल्ला में गतिविधि सब भेल आ छात्र, इरास्मस के विद्वान आ पूर्व छात्र, उद्यमी, नागरिक समाज के संगठन, नवीनता, निजी क्षेत्र के भागीदार आ युवा नेता सब के एक ठाम आनल गेल, यूरोपीय विदेश कार्य सेवा (ईईएएस) के हवाला स नेपाल में यूरोपीय संघ के प्रतिनिधिमंडल शुक्रदिन घोषणा केलक।

ई कार्यक्रम म॑ इरास्मस मुंडस प्री-डिपार्चर ओरिएंटेशन, ईयू यूथ फेस्ट आरू ईयू यूथ एलुमनी डे के संयोजन करलऽ गेलऽ छेलै ।

नेपालमे ईयूके राजदूत वेरोनिक लोरेन्जो इरास्मस मुण्डस संयुक्त मास्टर डिग्री छात्रवृत्ति प्राप्त कएने ४२ नेपाली छात्रसभके सम्पूर्ण ईयूके विश्वविद्यालयमे पढयके लेल बधाई देलनि ।

प्राप्तकर्ता म॑ २२ महिला आरू २० पुरुष शामिल छेलै, आरू ई जनस्वास्थ्य, साइबर सुरक्षा, पत्रकारिता, अक्षय ऊर्जा आरू टिकाऊ निर्माण जैसनऽ विषयऽ के अध्ययन करतै ।

ईयू यूथ फेस्ट २०२६ म॑ १५०० स॑ भी अधिक युवा न॑ भाग लेलकै, जेकरा म॑ प्रतिभागी सिनी क॑ पेशेवरऽ स॑ मार्गदर्शन आरू मार्गदर्शन मिललै आरू थ्रीडी मॉडलिंग आरू प्रिंटिंग, ड्रोन सिमुलेशन आरू एआई संचालित गेम सहित गतिविधियऽ के कोशिश करलऽ गेलै ।

ई आयोजन म॑ एनीमेशन, रोबोटिक्स आरू आर्टिफिशियल इंटेलिजेंस सहित उभरतऽ उद्योगऽ स॑ भी परिचय कराय देलऽ गेलै ।

19.1 लाख यूरो के नव अनुदान के घोषणा

प्रतिनिधिमंडल न॑ कहलकै कि ई महोत्सव म॑ संयुक्त रूप स॑ १.९१ मिलियन यूरो के दू नया अनुदान शुरू करलऽ गेलै — डिजिटल अर्थव्यवस्था म॑ युवा लेली अवसर पैदा करना (कोडे) आरू नेपाली युवा सिनी के डिजिटल एक्सेलरेशन आरू महत्वाकांक्षा क॑ उजागर करना (यूडीएएन) ।

कोड स्विसकोन्टैक्ट, रेस्टलेस डेवलपमेंट आ नेपाल रोबोटिक्स एसोसिएशन द्वारा लागू कएल जाएत, जखन कि यूडीएएन यूथ इनोवेशन लैब, वीमेन इन एनीमेशन, हेफर प्रोजेक्ट नेपाल आ नेपाल एप्लाइड मैथमेटिक्स एंड इन्फोर्मैटिक्स इंस्टीट्यूट फॉर रिसर्च (नामआईआई) द्वारा देल जायत।

ई पहलऽ म॑ नेपाल केरऽ सात प्रांतऽ के युवा सिनी क॑ संलग्न करलऽ जैतै, जेकरा म॑ डिजिटल कौशल, रोजगार क्षमता, उद्यमिता आरू नवीनता प॑ ध्यान देलऽ जैतै, जेकरा म॑ युवा महिला, ग्रामीण समुदाय, आरू कमजोर आरू हाशिया प॑ पड़लऽ समूहऽ प॑ विशेष ध्यान देलऽ जैतै ।

लोरेन्जो कहलनि जे, नेपालक एकटा पैघ संसाधन अछि ओकर युवा। ओ आगू कहलीह जे मुदा एहि संभावना क बराबरी कौशल, अवसर आ रोजगार मे निवेश स करबाक चाही।

ईयू न॑ ईयू केरऽ युवा पूर्व छात्र दिवस भी आयोजित करलकै, जेकरा म॑ पूर्व छात्र, युवा संगठन आरू भागीदारऽ क॑ एक साथ लानी क॑ सर्कुलर अर्थव्यवस्था, हरित विकास, शिक्षा, जलवायु कार्रवाई आरू युवा भागीदारी सहित क्षेत्रऽ म॑ युवा नेतृत्व वाला पहलऽ के प्रदर्शन करलऽ गेलै ।

title: Nepal Reimagined: Inside the Himalayas' New Era of Rarefied Travel - Luxury Travel Magazine
description: Nepal Reimagined: Inside the Himalayas' New Era of Rarefied Travel  Luxury Travel Magazine
publisher.title: Luxury Travel Magazine
full_article:
There is a particular kind of silence that exists only above 4,000 metres, the hush that settles over a helicopter cabin the instant the rotors clear Kathmandu's haze and the first white ridgeline of the Himalaya breaks the horizon. For decades, Nepal has been synonymous with hardship travel: weeks of trekking, teahouse dormitories, and the quiet suffering that comes with earning a mountain view the old-fashioned way.

That Nepal still exists, and it still has its devotees. But a different Nepal has been quietly taking shape alongside it one built for travellers who want the Himalaya's grandeur without surrendering the comforts they've grown accustomed to elsewhere in the world.

This is the Nepal of heritage palaces reborn as five-star hotels, of private jungle lodges where leopards pad past your veranda at dawn, of Newari tasting menus served in seventeenth-century courtyards, and most dramatically of helicopters that turn a three-week expedition into a single unforgettable morning. For the modern luxury traveller, Nepal in 2026 is no longer a question of endurance. It is a question of curation.

A Country Built for the Vertical Escape

Nepal's geography is its own best marketing department. Within a single small nation sit eight of the world's fourteen peaks above 8,000 metres, subtropical jungle teeming with rhinos and Bengal tigers, terraced hill country dotted with monasteries older than most European nations, and a capital valley whose temple squares have been continuously inhabited for over a thousand years. Few destinations on earth offer such violent contrast in such tight geographic proximity, a fact that has not been lost on the operators now reshaping how travellers experience it.

What has changed is accessibility. Improved regional airstrips, a fast-growing charter aviation sector, and a new generation of design-forward lodges have collapsed the distance between "remote" and "reachable." A guest can breakfast at a heritage hotel in Kathmandu, land beside Everest before lunch, and be soaking in a hot stone bath overlooking Phewa Lake in Pokhara by evening. That itinerary would have been unthinkable, or at least deeply unwise, a generation ago.

The Helicopter Advantage: Nepal's Real Luxury Currency

If there is a single symbol of Nepal's shift toward rarefied travel, it is the helicopter. Where trekking to Everest Base Camp traditionally demands twelve to fourteen days of high-altitude walking, acclimatisation stops, and no small amount of physical suffering, a private helicopter closes that same distance in a matter of hours, and does so while delivering a vantage point that no trekker, however fit, will ever achieve on foot.

A typical Everest helicopter tour experience departs Kathmandu's Tribhuvan International Airport in the stillness of early morning, when mountain air is calmest and visibility is at its sharpest. The route threads over the forested ridgelines of the Solukhumbu, past the dramatic airstrip at Lukla, over the Sherpa capital of Namche Bazaar, and on toward Everest itself, with Lhotse, Nuptse and Ama Dablam unfolding in sequence through the cabin windows. Many itineraries include a landing near Everest Base Camp or at Kala Patthar, followed by a breakfast stop at one of the highest hotels on the planet, its dining room offering an uninterrupted panorama of the world's tallest mountain. The return leg back to Kathmandu typically wraps the entire experience into a half-day outing, extraordinary altitude and extraordinary scenery, compressed into the length of a long brunch.

Everest is only the beginning. The Annapurna Sanctuary, the sacred lakes of Gosaikunda, the remote kingdom of Upper Mustang with its cave monasteries and wind-carved cliffs, and even short scenic loops over the Kathmandu Valley's medieval cities are all increasingly accessed by air. For travellers with limited time, mobility concerns, or simply no interest in weeks of tent camping, the helicopter has become less a novelty and more the default way serious travellers now experience the Himalaya.

It is worth noting that not all helicopter experiences in Nepal are created equal. The market has split into two distinct tiers: shared-seat departures that fill a helicopter with several unrelated parties on a fixed schedule, and fully private charters built entirely around one group's pace, photography preferences, and choice of landing points. The difference shows up in everything from how long the aircraft is permitted to linger over a particular ridge to whether the pilot circles back for the shot you actually wanted. For a magazine audience accustomed to bespoke travel, the private charter is almost always the better investment, and it is the only way to guarantee the departure time, route, and landing sequence are built around you rather than a manifest of strangers.

This is where planning ahead matters enormously. Himalayan flying is entirely weather-dependent, mountain air is unforgiving of poor scheduling, and the best aircraft and pilots are booked out well in advance during the prime spring and autumn seasons. Travellers serious about building a Nepal itinerary around a helicopter centrepiece, whether that's a private Everest breakfast flight, a scenic loop over Annapurna, or a multi-day heli-trekking combination, are best served by booking through a specialist rather than assembling the logistics themselves.

Aero Connect Nepal has emerged as one of the more established names in this space, coordinating private and shared helicopter charters across the Everest, Annapurna, and Langtang regions, with the flexibility to build custom routes, landing sequences, and combined heli-and-lodge itineraries for travellers who want the experience designed around them rather than the other way around. Booking several months ahead of a spring or autumn departure is strongly advised, both to secure aircraft availability and to build in the flexibility that Himalayan weather inevitably demands.

Where to Rest: Nepal's New Generation of Heritage and Wilderness Hotels

A helicopter can deliver you to the mountains in an afternoon, but it is where you rest afterward that defines whether a trip feels like an adventure or a genuine escape. Nepal's hospitality scene has matured considerably over the past decade, and nowhere is that more visible than in Kathmandu itself, where a handful of heritage properties have restored centuries-old brick-and-timber architecture into some of Asia's more distinctive hotels. Courtyards built in the Newari style, hand-carved wooden windows, and slow, deliberate design stand in deliberate contrast to the glass-and-marble language of international hotel chains, offering a sense of place that a standard five-star simply cannot replicate.

Beyond the capital, Pokhara has become the country's soft-adventure base camp, a lakeside city framed by the Annapurna range, where paragliding, boating on Phewa Lake, and a growing cluster of boutique lodges give travellers a gentler counterpoint to the high mountains. Further into the hills, a small number of luxury trekking lodges now offer heated rooms, curated wine lists, and mountain views that rival anything reachable on foot, aimed squarely at travellers who want proximity to the Himalaya without renouncing comfort.

To the south, Chitwan National Park offers an entirely different Nepal, dense sal forest, oxbow lakes, and healthy populations of one-horned rhinoceros and, increasingly, Bengal tiger. A small collection of safari lodges here now rival East Africa's finest camps, offering private jeep and canoe excursions, riverside dining, and the kind of unhurried wildlife encounters that reward patience over spectacle. For travellers building a comprehensive Nepal itinerary, pairing a mountain-focused opening chapter with a jungle-based closing chapter has become an increasingly popular structure, high-altitude adrenaline followed by lowland stillness.

And for the truly adventurous, Upper Mustang remains one of the last genuinely remote corners of the Himalaya open to outside visitors, a former forbidden kingdom of red cliffs, whitewashed monasteries, and a culture more closely tied to Tibet than to the Kathmandu Valley below. Access here is improving but remains deliberately limited, which is precisely its appeal to travellers who have already exhausted the more conventional luxury circuits elsewhere in the world.

Culture and Cuisine: The Layer That Makes Nepal Unforgettable

It would be a mistake to treat Nepal as purely a landscape destination. The Kathmandu Valley alone holds seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites within a radius of barely twenty kilometres, the medieval Durbar Squares of Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur, the enormous white stupa at Boudhanath, the hilltop temple complex of Swayambhunath, and the sacred Hindu site of Pashupatinath among them.

A private historian-led tour through these sites, ideally timed for early morning before the crowds arrive, remains one of the most rewarding ways to spend a day in the capital, and pairs naturally with a helicopter itinerary that otherwise focuses purely on mountain scenery.

Nepali cuisine, too, has entered a period of genuine reinvention. Newari cooking, the cuisine of the Kathmandu Valley's original inhabitants, has begun appearing on tasting menus at a handful of fine-dining restaurants, presenting centuries-old recipes with a level of plating and precision previously reserved for European capitals. Expect buffalo and duck preparations, fermented and pickled vegetables, and a complexity of spice that rewards slow, multi-course exploration rather than a quick meal between excursions.

Practical Notes for the Discerning Traveller

Most travellers from the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union, Canada, and Australia can obtain a visa on arrival or a straightforward e-visa, making Nepal considerably more accessible than its remote reputation suggests. The prime travel windows remain spring (March to May) and autumn (late September to November), when skies are clearest and mountain flying is at its most reliable, though it is worth building a day or two of scheduling flexibility into any itinerary anchored around a helicopter departure, since Himalayan weather can ground flights on short notice regardless of season.

For travellers assembling a full Nepal itinerary, a sensible structure has emerged among specialist operators: two to three nights in Kathmandu for culture, cuisine, and a private mountain helicopter excursion; a transfer to Pokhara or a luxury trekking lodge for a gentler pace and Annapurna views; and a closing chapter in Chitwan for wildlife, before departure. Those with additional time increasingly extend into Upper Mustang or combine a heli-trek flying in, walking a shorter, curated section of trail, and flying back out, for a taste of the trekking experience without its full physical toll.

The Bottom Line

Nepal has spent half a century being sold to the world as a test of endurance. What is emerging now is a different proposition entirely: a country whose extraordinary geography, layered culture, and improving infrastructure make it one of the more compelling additions to the modern luxury circuit.

The helicopter, more than any single hotel or lodge, is what has made this shift possible, collapsing weeks of hardship into hours of spectacle, and putting Everest itself within reach of a traveller who has no interest in ever pitching a tent.

For those ready to build that itinerary, the first booking worth making is often the aircraft. Specialist operators such as AeroConnect Nepal offer the private charter flexibility that a bespoke Himalayan trip demands and with prime spring and autumn slots filling months in advance, it is the one reservation in a Nepal itinerary that rewards being made early.
